```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Mistry_2018_vemurafenib_tumor"))$reference`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1007/s00280-017-3486-3> (open access, PMC5778167)
* Supplement: Electronic Supplementary Material 1 (model-development Tables S1-S3
  and the final parameter Table S4).

Mistry, Orrell and Eftimie fitted the same piecewise-linear mixed-effects model
separately to the target-lesion data of three phase III trials in BRAF-mutant
metastatic melanoma: the vemurafenib arm of BRIM-3, the dabrafenib arm of
BREAK-3 and the trametinib arm of METRIC. The three fits are independent, so the
package ships one model per drug:

```{r models}
drugs <- c("vemurafenib", "dabrafenib", "trametinib")
model_names <- paste0("Mistry_2018_", drugs, "_tumor")
mods <- lapply(model_names, function(nm) rxode2::rxode(readModelDb(nm)))
names(mods) <- drugs
for (d in drugs) cat(d, ":", mods[[d]]$description, "\n\n")
```

## Structure

Following Mayneord, the authors argue that a tumour grows from a thin
proliferating rim, so its radius (and longest diameter) changes linearly in
time rather than exponentially. Each lesion's longest diameter L is modelled as

* L = BSL + d t, for t < sp
* L = BSL + d sp + g t, for t >= sp

with baseline diameter BSL, shrinkage slope d, regrowth slope g (mm/day), and a
population switch time sp = 63 days shared by all three drugs. log(BSL), d and g
each carry two independent normal random effects: a between-patient (BP) effect
shared by all lesions of a patient and a within-patient (WP) effect specific to
each lesion. For vemurafenib the variance of g shrank to zero during model
development, so g is a fixed effect only.

In the packaged models the patient is the rxode2 `ID` and the lesion is the
`LESION` column. The BP etas (`etalrbase`, `etaslope_shrink`,
`etaslope_regrow`) are ordinary subject-level etas; the WP etas
(`etalrbase_lesion`, ...) are declared `~ var | LESION`, which gives every lesion
of every patient its own draw. The observation `tumor_size` is the longest
diameter of a single lesion in mm.

# Population

The analysis population is the patients of each phase III arm whose first
on-treatment scan (week 6) showed stable disease, partial or complete response:
203 on vemurafenib, 165 on dabrafenib and 157 on trametinib (Mistry 2018 Table
1). The authors restricted the analysis to RECIST target lesions and refer to the
original trial publications (Chapman 2011, Hauschild 2012, Flaherty 2012) for
demographics, which this paper does not tabulate. Baseline sum of longest
diameters (SLD) had medians of 72, 62 and 64 mm, and the week-6 objective
response rate in the analysis population was 60%, 63% and 29%. About 80% of
patients had more than one target lesion (Figure 3).

```{r population}
str(readModelDb("Mistry_2018_dabrafenib_tumor")()$population)
```

# Source trace

| Equation / parameter | Vemurafenib | Dabrafenib | Trametinib | Source location |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Piecewise-linear lesion model | | | | Methods, equations for L_ijk |
| `lrbase` (mean log BSL, log mm) | 3.38 | 3.25 | 3.22 | Table S4, log(BSL) mean |
| `etalrbase` (BP variance) | 0.41^2 | 0.26^2 | 0.26^2 | Table S4, log(BSL) s.d. (BP) |
| `etalrbase_lesion` (WP variance) | 0.34^2 | 0.40^2 | 0.42^2 | Table S4, log(BSL) s.d. (WP) |
| `slope_shrink` (d, mm/day) | -0.26 | -0.24 | -0.13 | Table S4, d mean |
| `etaslope_shrink` (BP variance) | 0.38^2 | 0.11^2 | 0.09^2 | Table S4, d s.d. (BP) |
| `etaslope_shrink_lesion` (WP variance) | 0.32^2 | 0.11^2 | 0.13^2 | Table S4, d s.d. (WP) |
| `slope_regrow` (g, mm/day) | 0.02 | 0.06 | 0.05 | Table S4, g mean |
| `etaslope_regrow` (BP variance) | none | 0.09^2 | 0.12^2 | Table S4, g s.d. (BP); NA for vemurafenib |
| `etaslope_regrow_lesion` (WP variance) | none | 0.07^2 | 0.03^2 | Table S4, g s.d. (WP); NA for vemurafenib |
| `tregrow` (sp, day) | 63 (fixed) | 63 (fixed) | 63 (fixed) | Table S4 SP; Methods (grid 63 / 116 / 179); Tables S1-S3 |
| `addSd` (mm) | 0 (fixed) | 0 (fixed) | 0 (fixed) | not reported (see Assumptions) |
| Final model | Table S1 Model 16 | Table S2 Model 8 | Table S3 Model 8 | Supplement |

# Between- and within-patient variability (Figure 5)

Figure 5 of the paper plots the coefficient of variation (s.d. divided by the
mean) of the shrinkage and regrowth slopes. Recomputing it from the packaged
`ini()` values checks that the Table S4 standard deviations were entered as
variances on the right parameters. The reference values are the point estimates
read off Figure 5.

```{r fig5}
cv_from_model <- function(mod, eta, theta) {
  om <- mod$omega
  v <- if (eta %in% rownames(om$id)) om$id[eta, eta] else om$LESION[eta, eta]
  100 * sqrt(v) / abs(mod$theta[[theta]])
}
fig5 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~drug, ~slope, ~level, ~eta, ~theta, ~cv_fig5,
  "vemurafenib", "shrinkage", "between patient", "etaslope_shrink", "slope_shrink", 146,
  "vemurafenib", "shrinkage", "within patient", "etaslope_shrink_lesion", "slope_shrink", 122,
  "dabrafenib", "shrinkage", "between patient", "etaslope_shrink", "slope_shrink", 46,
  "dabrafenib", "shrinkage", "within patient", "etaslope_shrink_lesion", "slope_shrink", 46,
  "trametinib", "shrinkage", "between patient", "etaslope_shrink", "slope_shrink", 69,
  "trametinib", "shrinkage", "within patient", "etaslope_shrink_lesion", "slope_shrink", 99,
  "dabrafenib", "regrowth", "between patient", "etaslope_regrow", "slope_regrow", 154,
  "dabrafenib", "regrowth", "within patient", "etaslope_regrow_lesion", "slope_regrow", 113,
  "trametinib", "regrowth", "between patient", "etaslope_regrow", "slope_regrow", 249,
  "trametinib", "regrowth", "within patient", "etaslope_regrow_lesion", "slope_regrow", 60
)
fig5$cv_model <- mapply(
  function(d, e, th) cv_from_model(mods[[d]], e, th),
  fig5$drug, fig5$eta, fig5$theta
)
fig5 |>
  mutate(cv_model = round(cv_model, 1)) |>
  dplyr::select(drug, slope, level, cv_fig5, cv_model) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Drug" = drug, "Slope" = slope, "Level" = level,
    "CV read off Figure 5 (%)" = cv_fig5, "CV from model (%)" = cv_model
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

# Deterministic: the CVs follow from Table S4 by arithmetic, so only the
# reading precision of Figure 5 (a few percent) separates the two columns.
# An SD entered as a variance (or the reverse) would miss by a factor.
stopifnot(all(abs(fig5$cv_model / fig5$cv_fig5 - 1) < 0.06))
# Shrinkage-slope variability: vemurafenib > trametinib > dabrafenib.
cv_bp <- with(subset(fig5, slope == "shrinkage" & level == "between patient"), setNames(cv_model, drug))
stopifnot(cv_bp[["vemurafenib"]] > cv_bp[["trametinib"]], cv_bp[["trametinib"]] > cv_bp[["dabrafenib"]])
# Vemurafenib carries no random effect on the regrowth slope.
stopifnot(!any(grepl("regrow", c(rownames(mods$vemurafenib$omega$id), rownames(mods$vemurafenib$omega$LESION)))))
```

The model reproduces the ordering the paper reports: shrinkage-slope variability
is largest for vemurafenib, then trametinib, then dabrafenib.

# Typical lesion trajectories

The typical-value lesion (all random effects zero) starts at exp(`lrbase`) mm.
Because the published regrowth arm is `d sp + g t` rather than
`d sp + g (t - sp)`, the trajectory steps up by g x 63 mm at day 63 (1.3, 3.8 and
3.2 mm for the three drugs). The dashed line shows the continuous alternative
for comparison only; the packaged model follows the printed equation.

```{r typical}
lesion_events <- function(n_les, times) {
  tidyr::crossing(id = 1L, LESION = seq_len(n_les), time = times) |>
    mutate(evid = 0L) |>
    arrange(id, time, LESION)
}
times_fine <- seq(0, 280, by = 1)
typ <- bind_rows(lapply(drugs, function(d) {
  s <- rxode2::rxSolve(
    rxode2::zeroRe(mods[[d]]),
    lesion_events(2L, times_fine),
    returnType = "data.frame"
  )
  s |> filter(LESION == 1) |> mutate(drug = d)
}))
th <- bind_rows(lapply(drugs, function(d) {
  tibble(
    drug = d, bsl = exp(mods[[d]]$theta[["lrbase"]]),
    dd = mods[[d]]$theta[["slope_shrink"]], gg = mods[[d]]$theta[["slope_regrow"]]
  )
}))
hinge <- tidyr::crossing(th, time = times_fine) |>
  mutate(ld_hinge = bsl + dd * pmin(time, 63) + gg * pmax(time - 63, 0))

ggplot(typ, aes(time, tumor_size, colour = drug)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = hinge, aes(time, ld_hinge, colour = drug), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 63, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(
    x = "Time since start of treatment (day)",
    y = "Typical lesion longest diameter (mm)",
    colour = NULL,
    caption = "Solid: packaged model (printed equation). Dashed: continuous-hinge alternative."
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

The typical-lesion percentage change at the week-6 scan (day 42) can be set
against the median percentage change in SLD in Table 1. The two are not the same
statistic (one lesion versus a patient's sum), but with a linear model and a
median patient they should agree to a few percentage points.

```{r typical-week6}
wk6_typ <- typ |>
  group_by(drug) |>
  summarise(
    pct = 100 * (tumor_size[time == 42] / tumor_size[time == 0] - 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    tibble(drug = drugs, pct_table1 = c(-34, -39, -18)),
    by = "drug"
  ) |>
  mutate(drug = factor(drug, levels = drugs)) |>
  arrange(drug)
wk6_typ |>
  mutate(pct = round(pct, 1)) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Drug" = drug,
    "Typical lesion change at day 42 (%)" = pct,
    "Table 1 median SLD change at week 6 (%)" = pct_table1
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

# Deterministic typical-value solve: a mis-transcribed baseline or slope moves
# this by tens of percentage points.
stopifnot(all(abs(wk6_typ$pct - wk6_typ$pct_table1) < 5))
```

# Virtual cohort

Each arm is simulated with the number of target lesions per patient taken from
Figure 3 of the paper. The vemurafenib arm (203 patients) is thinned
evenly to 200 patients to keep within the vignette's per-arm cohort cap,
preserving the lesion-count distribution. Imaging visits are the on-treatment
visits named in the Methods (days 42, 84, 147 and 210) plus baseline.

```{r cohort}
lesion_counts <- list(
  # Figure 3: number of patients with 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, (6), 7 target lesions
  vemurafenib = c(39, 55, 40, 47, 21, 0, 1),
  dabrafenib = c(34, 56, 29, 26, 20),
  trametinib = c(31, 42, 34, 23, 27)
)
visits <- c(0, 42, 84, 147, 210)

make_cohort <- function(counts, n_max = 200L) {
  n_les <- rep(seq_along(counts), counts)
  if (length(n_les) > n_max) {
    n_les <- n_les[round(seq(1, length(n_les), length.out = n_max))]
  }
  tibble(id = seq_along(n_les), n_les = n_les) |>
    rowwise() |>
    reframe(id = id, LESION = seq_len(n_les)) |>
    tidyr::crossing(time = visits) |>
    mutate(evid = 0L) |>
    arrange(id, time, LESION)
}

rxode2::rxSetSeed(2018)
sim <- bind_rows(lapply(drugs, function(d) {
  ev <- make_cohort(lesion_counts[[d]])
  s <- rxode2::rxSolve(mods[[d]], ev, omega = mods[[d]]$omega, returnType = "data.frame")
  s |> mutate(drug = d)
}))
sim |>
  distinct(drug, id) |>
  count(drug, name = "patients") |>
  knitr::kable()
```

# Individual lesion time courses (Figure 2)

Figure 2 of the paper shows the individual longest diameters of all lesions at
each imaging visit. The packaged model is linear in time, so a lesion with a
small baseline and a steep shrinkage slope can be predicted below zero; those
predictions are shown at 0 mm, the value a disappeared lesion is recorded as.

```{r fig2}
sim |>
  mutate(ild = pmax(tumor_size, 0), drug = factor(drug, levels = drugs)) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, ild)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 4, height = 0, alpha = 0.3, shape = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~drug) +
  labs(x = "Days", y = "ILD (mm)") +
  theme_bw()
```

# Week-6 response (Table 1)

Patient SLD is the sum over that patient's simulated lesions (negative
predictions set to 0 mm). The objective response at week 6 is a decrease of SLD
by at least 30% from baseline (RECIST partial or complete response).

```{r table1}
sld <- sim |>
  mutate(ld = pmax(tumor_size, 0)) |>
  group_by(drug, id, time) |>
  summarise(sld = sum(ld), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(drug, id) |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * (sld / sld[time == 0] - 1)) |>
  ungroup()

tab1 <- sld |>
  group_by(drug) |>
  summarise(
    sld0_med = median(sld[time == 0]),
    sld0_q25 = quantile(sld[time == 0], 0.25),
    sld0_q75 = quantile(sld[time == 0], 0.75),
    pct_med = median(pct[time == 42]),
    pct_q25 = quantile(pct[time == 42], 0.25),
    pct_q75 = quantile(pct[time == 42], 0.75),
    orr = 100 * mean(pct[time == 42] <= -30),
    pd = 100 * mean(pct[time == 42] >= 20),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    tibble(
      drug = drugs,
      sld0_pub = c("72 (39, 122)", "62 (34, 100)", "64 (32, 106)"),
      sld0_pub_med = c(72, 62, 64),
      pct_pub = c("-34 (-47, -21)", "-39 (-53, -22)", "-18 (-31, -4)"),
      pct_pub_med = c(-34, -39, -18),
      orr_pub = c(60, 63, 29)
    ),
    by = "drug"
  ) |>
  mutate(drug = factor(drug, levels = drugs)) |>
  arrange(drug)

tab1 |>
  mutate(
    sld0_sim = sprintf("%.0f (%.0f, %.0f)", sld0_med, sld0_q25, sld0_q75),
    pct_sim = sprintf("%.0f (%.0f, %.0f)", pct_med, pct_q25, pct_q75),
    orr_sim = round(orr),
    pd_sim = round(pd)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(drug, sld0_pub, sld0_sim, pct_pub, pct_sim, orr_pub, orr_sim, pd_sim) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Drug" = drug,
    "Baseline SLD, Table 1 (mm)" = sld0_pub,
    "Baseline SLD, simulated (mm)" = sld0_sim,
    "Week-6 SLD change, Table 1 (%)" = pct_pub,
    "Week-6 SLD change, simulated (%)" = pct_sim,
    "Week-6 ORR, Table 1 (%)" = orr_pub,
    "Week-6 ORR, simulated (%)" = orr_sim,
    "Week-6 SLD increase >= 20%, simulated (%)" = pd_sim
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

pct_bound <- c(vemurafenib = 22, dabrafenib = 12, trametinib = 12)
stopifnot(
  # Baseline SLD centre: lesion-count distribution x baseline-diameter model.
  # Across 40 random cohorts the simulated median ran 2% below to 29% above
  # Table 1; a baseline entered on the wrong scale misses by far more.
  all(abs(tab1$sld0_med / tab1$sld0_pub_med - 1) < 0.4),
  # Week-6 response centre. Vemurafenib's shrinkage-slope variance is large,
  # so its cohort median moved from 11 points below to 17 points above Table 1
  # across 40 random cohorts of 200 (dabrafenib and trametinib within 9
  # points). The tight check is the deterministic typical-lesion comparison
  # above; this one catches a slope off by a factor.
  all(abs(tab1$pct_med - tab1$pct_pub_med) < pct_bound[as.character(tab1$drug)]),
  # Trametinib shrinks least: at least 9 points above dabrafenib in every one
  # of the 40 cohorts.
  tab1$pct_med[tab1$drug == "trametinib"] > tab1$pct_med[tab1$drug == "dabrafenib"] + 3
)
```

The medians of baseline SLD and of the week-6 SLD change are in the range of
Table 1 for all three drugs; the simulated baseline SLD tends to run somewhat
above the published median. The cohort median for vemurafenib varies most
between random cohorts. For vemurafenib in particular, the simulated spread of
the week-6 change is wider than published, and some simulated patients have an
SLD increase of 20% or more at week 6. The analysis population excluded patients
with progressive disease at the first scan, so the observed data cannot contain
such patients; the model, fitted with unrestricted normal slopes, does not
impose this selection. This is a property of the published model, not a
transcription issue.

# Shrinkage versus regrowth slopes (Figure 6)

Figure 6 plots the individual decay and regrowth rates of each lesion for
trametinib and dabrafenib and finds no correlation. Because the published
random effects are independent, the simulated lesion-level slopes are
uncorrelated by construction. The simulated spread is wider than in Figure 6,
which shows shrunken empirical Bayes estimates.

```{r fig6}
sim |>
  filter(drug != "vemurafenib", time == 0) |>
  mutate(drug = factor(drug, levels = c("trametinib", "dabrafenib"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(slope_regrow_i, slope_shrink_i)) +
  geom_point(shape = 1, alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~drug, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Re-growth rate (mm/day)", y = "Decay rate (mm/day)") +
  theme_bw()
```

# NCA

The model has no pharmacokinetic component: drug exposure is not an input, and
the treatment effect is absorbed into the empirical slopes. A PKNCA analysis
therefore does not apply. The validation above uses the paper's own summary
statistics (Table 1, Figures 3 and 5) instead.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Regrowth arm as printed.** Both equations for L in the Methods give the
  regrowth arm as `BSL + d sp + g t`, not `BSL + d sp + g (t - sp)`, so the
  model has a step of `g sp` (1.3-3.8 mm for a typical lesion) at day 63. The
  printed equation is followed. The second equation writes the switch time as
  `s_ij`, but the text states that sp could not vary across lesions and was
  chosen from a grid, so a single fixed `tregrow` is used.
* **Residual error not reported.** The model includes an additive residual
  error e_ijk, but its standard deviation appears nowhere in the article or the
  supplement. `addSd` is fixed to 0, so simulations are of the individual
  predicted diameters. Add a residual error before using the model to fit data.
* **Negative diameters.** Like the published model, the packaged model places
  no floor on the predicted diameter. The vignette sets negative predictions to
  0 mm when computing SLD; the model output itself is left unmodified.
* **Switch time fixed.** sp = 63 days was chosen from the grid 63 / 116 / 179
  days by log-likelihood and is encoded as `fixed()`.
* **Nesting column.** The patient is the rxode2 `ID` and the lesion is the
  `LESION` column, which rxode2 uses only as the nesting level of the
  within-patient random effects. An event table must contain at least two
  distinct `LESION` values.
* **Table 1 ILD.** Table 1 reports a median individual longest diameter of
  17-21 mm, below the exp(`lrbase`) of 25-29 mm and the simulated baseline lesion
  median. The table does not say at which visits ILD was summarised; the
  baseline SLD is close to the simulation, so the ILD row was not used as
  a validation target.
* **Dosing.** The paper does not state the doses of the three trials, and dose
  is not a model input.
* **Cohort thinning.** The vemurafenib cohort was thinned from 203 to 200
  patients for the vignette's cohort cap.
